external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)

The details that look like plumbing are tested because they are not — a press moves first (or a hover-dependent page is clicked in the wrong place), a drag reports the button held (or it ends halfway through), a cancel releases (or the page keeps a press the finger has left), text is inserted rather than typed (or an IME's word arrives as nonsense), and a scroll detent is a proportion of the viewport rather than a pixel count. rows.name: IME
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host that can answer the signalling URL (RB-010)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: The surface declares itself a text editor, so the IME opens for the remote page's fields — a renderer with a touch listener never does, and the symptom is the caret appearing on the far side with no keyboard on the phone. Composition and commit are separate kinds on purpose: an IME that produced one word from five keystrokes did not produce five keys, and replaying it as keys is how non-Latin input arrives as nonsense. Backspace is sent as a key rather than as a surrounding-text edit, because the remote page owns where its caret is. Not executed anywhere: an InputConnection needs an IME.

rows.name: native address/search
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host that answers a real SDP offer (RB-002/RB-010)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: §17.2. The classification is local and the *result* travels, so the host is told "navigate here" or "search for this" rather than handed raw text to guess about — a host that guessed would guess differently from the bar the owner is looking at. Navigation goes through the input path as §17.2 requires, which needed six new protocol kinds on both sides rather than a REST route: an address bar that could navigate by calling the Gateway would be a way round the control lease. Suggestions are OFF by default and the composable has no path to change it; a URL and anything carrying a credential are never sent even under consent. Adding the kinds to the shared enum immediately broke a downstream invariant, which is the system working: the Stream Host's input router asserts that every kind has a CDP mapping and that it emits `Input.*` and nothing else. Both cannot be true of a navigation, so the router refuses one by its own name — a boundary, not a gap. Collapsing it into "kind has no mapping" would invite the next reader to close it by adding `Page.navigate` to the table, which is the one method that router must never emit; navigation is handed to the Browser Control Agent's `navigate` operation instead, which owns the scheme allowlist and the step budget.

Every ordering a lossy channel produces is executed — an update before its create, a close for the active tab, an activation for a target nobody announced. §17.6's Back order is here too, and its last clause is the one that matters: Back does not close the browser while the page has history.

rows.name: BrowserTask Mission binding regression proof
external_gates: a Browser Stream Host that runs the control agent (RB-010/RB-115)
rows.note: This row is why regression proofs are worth writing. §23.1's own worked example — "Van, search this page and explain it" — had never once worked: `bind_browser_session` named the capability `browser.interactive.session`, no registry declared it, and the route called the binder unguarded, so every mission-bound session raised MISSION_CAPABILITY_NOT_PERMITTED as a 500. The capability is declared now (EXTERNAL_RUNTIME against the `browser_stream_host` probe), the route refuses cleanly and unwinds the session rather than stranding the owner's profile, and the proof covers all three of §23's claims: binding is by reference and adds no Mission, manual browsing has none at all, and a completed browser activity does not verify the Mission.

external_gates: the five STREAM_HOST metrics have no producer until a host exists (RB-010)

The six the Gateway owns are recorded by real call sites and carry `silence_is_normal`, because none of them can fire without a Stream Host and an alert nobody can clear is how the alerts that matter stop being read. The five the host owns are declared STREAM_HOST so a permanently empty scrape reads as "no host" rather than "no traffic", and a test asserts the Gateway cannot write them. rows.note:
§38's sixty-six scenarios, each with a status from §38's own vocabulary: 57 PASS, 9 BLOCKED_EXTERNAL, none `assumed`.

The register is data and the checker is what makes it evidence. Every PASS must cite a runnable pytest node id — resolved by walking the module's AST for the `Class::test` chain, not by looking for the name — and all 197 cited Python tests were executed. The first version of this register cited twenty-five tests that exist and cannot be run, which is what that check now refuses.

A PASS means the repository can demonstrate the refusal, not that a live Remote Browser has been attacked and survived. The register says so in those words.

rows.note:
§43's hundred and four requirements, each with a status: 60 REPOSITORY_PROVEN, 37 BLOCKED_EXTERNAL, 7 OWNER_DEPLOYMENT_DECISION.

The verdict is recomputed from the rows rather than written, and the checker fails if the stored one disagrees. That is the point of building it as a program: a verdict a person writes at the top of a ledger is written once and never re-derived, and this one cannot go stale.

REPOSITORY_COMPLETE_PENDING_EXTERNAL is the honest answer and it is not a near miss. Nothing in the Runtime, Performance or Stream/control groups can be proven here at all, because none of it exists to be proven against — and `REPOSITORY_PROVEN` is defined in the register itself as weaker than certification, so the sixty do not round up either.

rows.name: session resume handshake
external_gates: the Android app module is compiled only in CI; the session manager imports OkHttp and is not in the pure-Kotlin harness
rows.note:
P0-SESS-001. Both halves read as wired and the pair did not work. The Gateway grants `authoritative_path_epoch + 1` on every accepted resume and fences any envelope that does not carry it; the phone kept the epoch `/open` gave it and incremented a counter of its own on each socket failure.

The device resumes on `onOpen`, before anything has failed, so on a healthy first connect every owner message was refused with `session_path_epoch_stale` — on a session both sides reported as connected. The local counter was wrong in the other direction too: it agreed after one failure and one resume, and diverged permanently after two failures in a row, which is what a carrier handover on a moving train looks like.

Found by probing the running service, not by reading either side. Now pinned at the route and across the two languages, including the case that would have caught the original shape: the grant is adopted on an ordinary resume and not only on a failover.

The device never calls this route (see RB-035): `resume()` is reached only from the socket's `onOpen`. What is proven here is the Gateway's handshake, driven by route-level tests.

**Corrected at C16, one commit after C15 strengthened it.** The Gateway's half is live and route-tested and the device's decisions are executed in the harness — but `adoptCursor` is reached only from `resume()`, `resume()` only from the socket's `onOpen`, and the socket is only opened by `start()`. **Corrected after review.** The Gateway's half was right and the reconciliation was not, in two directions that cancelled out. The phone sent `inFlight.keys` — *message* ids — as `pending_command_ids`, the Gateway resolved each as a *command* id against the mission table, so every answer was `UNKNOWN`; and the phone then removed every key it had asked about, the unknowns included. `UNKNOWN` is the one answer that means resend, so every reconnect silently discarded every unacknowledged owner command. `SessionReconciliation` now produces the identity asked about and matches the answer by the same function, `submit` puts the command id on the envelope where the Gateway records it, and `_resume_snapshot` answers from §20.12's admission table — scoped to the asking session — when no mission exists. rows.note:
**Corrected at C16.** Two checkpoints made this outbox durable and then atomic, and neither noticed that nothing puts anything in it: `submit` has no caller, and `restoreOutbox` is reached only from `start()`. The app's store-and-forward is the pre-§20 path — `EncryptedCommandQueue` drained by `QueueReplayer` — which is live. §20.14's policy metadata rides on that queue's record correctly and is written by nobody.

§2.7 forbids a parallel replacement for `EncryptedCommandQueue`, so this is not one: §20.14's metadata rides on that queue's own record.

**Corrected after review.** The first version held those records in an in-memory `ArrayDeque` and never touched the queue at all — durable in name, and a process death lost the reconfirmation, expiry, attempt count and path while the command could survive. P0-SESS-003. One record and one write now, persisted before it is queued and forgotten only after the send returns.

Writing the restart tests found two more: the mapping silently dropped `commandId`, which is what §20.12 matches a restored command by, and a session envelope in the shared queue was dispatchable by the replayer — P0-SEC-002's shape, now a named refusal rather than a reliance on `commandTextOrNull` returning null.

**Corrected again at C15, after external review.** The adapter was `queue.remove(messageId)` then `queue.enqueue(...)` — and the review was right that a kill between them loses the command. Attacking it found the seam was worse than reported. `enqueue` mints its own row id, so the record was never keyed by the message id: that `remove` matched nothing and neither did `forget`, which means every delivered command stayed on disk and was re-sent after each restart. `enqueue` also de-duplicates on the idempotency key and returns the existing row, so a reconfirmation — the owner's "yes" — was discarded. And `EncryptedCommandQueue`'s own `persist` and `remove` were each two editors with asynchronous `apply()`: three non-atomic writes, not one.

`OutboxRecordStore.upsert` is now the operation, the adapter depends on that interface rather than on the queue, and the whole adapter is executed in the harness against a store that can be killed between operations. The restore reader was also `peekReady`, which drops a `NO_STALE_REPLAY` record once attempted — exactly the class a restore exists to recover (P1-SESS-007).

Split by who can measure what, which is the only honest way to split it. rows.name: request proof-of-possession
external_gates: an Android client that signs requests with the bound key (RB-103 Android half)
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: Both ends now exist and the signing input is compared across the two languages against vectors the gateway generated. The device sends r||s rather than DER on purpose: the gateway accepts both, but only the fixed-width spelling is a constant 64 bytes, and a DER signature whose r happens to start with a high bit gains a leading zero — the kind of difference that works for weeks.

rows.name: single-use bootstrap provisioning
external_gates: the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note: The device's two round trips are implemented: the gateway issues a challenge, the Keystore bakes it into the certificate, and the attestation is sent back. Two trips rather than one because a chain captured from another enrolment has to be useless here, which it is only if the challenge is inside it. The enrolment routes are the one thing the proof gate exempts, and a test pins that: a device cannot be asked to prove possession of the key it is creating.

rows.name: automated ADB owner-S24 provisioning tool
external_gates: the owner's S24 Ultra and a live Gateway; this is Gate 14's physical verification and no repository test substitutes for it
the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note:
ADR-RB-026's installer path. One call: the Gateway mints both single-use tokens and the attestation challenge and sets the expiry, so an installer cannot extend a provisioning window or reuse a token by asking for it.

The payload travels over ADB, through a shell, and can reach a device log. That is acceptable only because three properties hold at once — it expires in ten minutes, the Gateway consumes the tokens atomically, and it is not sufficient on its own without a hardware attestation (§0D.3). Remove any one and the channel stops being defensible, which is why each has a test that fails if it is relaxed.

rows.name: production manual-config removal
rows.producer: ProvisioningStatus and the read-only Connections card
rows.consumer: the owner, who is told what is set up rather than asked to set it up
external_gates: the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note:
P0-SEC-013. §0D.2 lists eleven fields the production build must not expose, and two of them shipped as text boxes on two screens: a Gateway address and a pairing code.

A box asking the owner to type a server address is a phishing surface with their whole assistant behind it — one convincing message and every command afterwards belongs to somebody else, with nothing on the phone looking wrong. Both forms are gone; `baseUrl`'s setter and `pairThisDevice` are private, so a new form cannot be written without editing the client.

The guard is on shape, not wording: a rebuild that dropped the labels would pass a text search, so the test refuses any editable field at all on those two screens.

rows.name: stable app-signing/device-binding gate
external_gates: the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
a production keystore the owner holds; the gate refuses a release without one and cannot supply it
rows.note:
§0D.3's binding is this package plus this app signing identity plus this hardware Keystore key plus this Gateway owner-device slot. The release gate now refuses the one identity that is never stable: Android generates a debug keystore per machine, so a release signed with one is signed by whichever machine built it — and two builds of the same application id signed differently cannot replace one another. The owner's first sideload failed with exactly that dialog (P2-AND-016).

Checked by name rather than by fingerprint, because the fingerprint is not knowable at configuration time and `androiddebugkey` is.

rows.name: Browser Control Agent private VCN RPC
rows.consumer: Stagehand and Browser Harness on Trading Core, over mTLS
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
rows.note: The narrow contract exists and its six checks are executed: caller identity, session, lease, generation, scope, step budget. The ordering is a tested property rather than a comment — a refused call leaves the CDP double untouched. The generation check is the one worth naming: a preempted lease keeps the id it was issued with, so an agent that checked the id alone would keep typing into a page the owner has taken back. Not live: there is no host and no Chromium.

rows.name: Trading Core → Stream Host mTLS control path
rows.consumer: the Trading Core services holding the issued client certificates
external_gates: a private VCN between Trading Core and the Stream Host
a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
client certificates distributed to the calling services
rows.note: The PKI script and the server context exist. The context requires a client certificate and trusts only the private control CA — never the system store, which is the failure the foreign-certificate check in qualify.sh is written for: that test certificate carries a *correct* common name and must be rejected on its chain, because a name is not a credential. Unwired: no VCN, no certificates issued, no listener started.

rows.name: raw CDP loopback/public-exposure proof
rows.producer: qualify.sh's cdp_not_public check and LoopbackCdp's constructor
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
qualify.sh returning GREEN on a real host
rows.note: Two halves, one of them done. The repository half: the Chromium unit pins --remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1 (not redundant — Chromium has defaulted to all interfaces when given only a port), and the CDP client refuses any endpoint that is not a loopback literal, including `localhost`, which resolves at connect time on a machine this process does not control. The runtime half is qualify.sh connecting to the debugging port on every global address, and it needs a host. It also checks the debugger is listening on loopback at all, because otherwise the exposure check passes on a machine where nothing is running.

rows.name: stream-host profile storage implementation
rows.producer: bootstrap.sh's profile volume step (§13.5 option A)
external_gates: a provisioned dual-homed Browser Stream Host (RB-002/RB-010)
an encrypted block device attached to the Stream Host
rows.note: Option A is chosen and recorded with its reasoning: Chromium executes on the Stream Host so the profile bytes must be there, while profile *authority* stays on Trading Core. Option B puts the owner's authenticated cookies on a wire between two hosts and makes lease enforcement the only thing preventing two Chromiums writing one profile. bootstrap.sh refuses to run without a block device rather than falling back to a plain directory, and qualify.sh reports RED for a mount that is not dm-crypt.

rows.name: release-build immutable connectivity validation
external_gates: the Android build is compiled only in CI; the AGP is unreachable in the audit container
rows.note:
§0D.2 removed every field the owner could type an endpoint into, so a release build with no connectivity trust anchor can never accept a manifest and can never be provisioned. It would install, open, and sit on "waiting for the installer" forever, with nothing anywhere saying why.

The format is checked and not merely the presence: a truncated build argument that carried no PEM parses to no keys at all, which is the same dead APK with a value that looks configured.
